questions: Which atom gives an electron, and which one gains it?
What charges do the two ions end up with?
segments.say: Ionic bonding: sodium gives an electron away. Watch the lone outer electron leave sodium (2,8,1) and land on chlorine (2,8,7). Both ions now have full outer shells, and their opposite charges pull them together - that pull is the ionic bond. Tell your partner: who gave, who gained, and what are the charges?

questions: Can you point at one NaCl molecule in the lattice?
What does the formula NaCl actually tell us?
segments.say: The ionic lattice. Follow the pattern as it builds: sodium, chloride, sodium, chloride, in every direction, billions of ions in one giant structure. Try to point at a single NaCl molecule - you cannot, because there are none. The formula only gives the ratio: one sodium for one chloride. Now check the worksheet question on why solid salt cannot conduct.

questions: How is sharing different from the transfer in scene 1?
Why do both chlorine atoms end up with eight outer electrons?
segments.say: Covalent bonding: sharing, not giving. Watch the two chlorine atoms come together and pool one electron each into a shared pair. Nobody lost an electron and nobody gained one - they share, and the joined atoms make one molecule. Say it with me: ionic gives, covalent shares.

questions: What carries the charge through a metal wire?
Why does a metal bend instead of shattering?
segments.say: Metallic bonding: a sea of electrons. Watch the outer electrons leave their atoms and drift through the whole lattice of positive ions. That moving sea carries charge, and the ion layers can slide while the sea holds on, so metals bend. Quick check with your partner: name one property each that the sea explains.

questions: What will you picture from now on when you see the formula NaCl?
How do you decide which bond a substance has?
segments.say: Check the thinking. Look at the lattice one last time: separate ions, one giant pattern, no molecules. Before we finish, work through the trap section of your student notes in pairs, then do the exit ticket on your own - and for every substance, ask the one question that sorts them all: what do the outer electrons do?
segments.watchFor: Table salt is made of NaCl molecules. Listen for students who describe salt as pairs or piles of molecules. Send them back to the lattice picture: Salt is a giant ionic lattice: NaCl just gives the ratio, there are no separate NaCl molecules.
